subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Arohi, and the thing I remember about my first month in the city is a plate of sweets. I'd moved into a hostel where I knew no one. On the third evening, a girl I'd only nodded to knocked and handed me a laddoo, saying, "It's my sister's engagement, so everyone gets one." I nearly said "no thanks" out of shyness. I took it. Later Kamal from the next room asked if I wanted to join their group for chai. I said yes, then panicked, then went. Afterwards I texted my mother that people here were kind. It felt like I'd been counted in, in a very small way. I said thank you three times, which they laughed about.

qa.q: How many times did Arohi say thank you?
qa.a: Arohi said thank you three times.

qa.q: How did Arohi read the laddoo and the chai invitation, and what was Arohi feeling?
qa.a: Arohi read them as signs of welcome and felt counted in, even though Arohi was nervous at first.

qa.q: What could Arohi do to keep building friendships in the hostel?
qa.a: Arohi could keep accepting small invitations, share something in return, and say thanks in a personal way.

qa.q: How might the girl who offered the laddoo have seen Arohi's hesitation?
qa.a: She might have thought Arohi was shy, and her friendly offer to everyone suggests she meant to include Arohi.

grounding: Arohi reads shared sweets and an invitation as welcome in a new hostel.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: From the next table in the hostel mess I watched the new girl, Minakshi, hold a small steel box of homemade sweets. She turned to the girls near her and said, "My mother sent these. Please take one." Sharmila, who had lived on that floor for two years, took one and said, "Thank you, this is so good. Where are you from?" Minakshi smiled properly for the first time and answered. Others leaned in. A girl from another state said thank you in her own language, and everyone asked what it meant. I don't know what Minakshi had felt earlier that day, but by the time the box was empty she was laughing with the rest.

qa.q: What was in Minakshi's steel box?
qa.a: There were homemade sweets in it.

qa.q: What might Minakshi have been feeling when she offered the sweets, and how can the observer tell her mood changed?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous about being new, and the observer can tell her mood changed because she smiled properly and later laughed with the others, though the observer can't be sure.

qa.q: What could a hostel resident do to make a newcomer feel welcome?
qa.a: They could accept the offer warmly, say thank you and ask about where the newcomer is from.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt about Minakshi's gesture?
qa.a: Sharmila probably felt touched and curious, since she thanked her and asked where she was from.

grounding: An observer sees a newcomer's shared sweets and thanks read as welcome, building friendship.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage:
Day one. On Baljeet's first evening in the Chennai hostel, far from Ludhiana, a girl from the next room, Rukmini, knocked with a steel box. "Murukku. My Amma's. Welcome." Baljeet was surprised, unsure if it was just politeness.
Day three. Rukmini knocked again, this time to invite her to the hostel's Pongal lunch. Baljeet hesitated, thinking she'd be in the way. Rukmini laughed. "No, no, you're coming. You're one of us now." At the lunch, three girls showed her how to eat off the banana leaf with her fingers. Baljeet felt her shoulders loosen for the first time since arriving.
Day ten. Baljeet's mother sent a box of pinnis from home. Baljeet went door to door with them, starting with Rukmini. "Thank you for the murukku. And for Pongal." Rukmini bit into one and closed her eyes. "Now we're even," she grinned. "But you're still coming to Karthigai."

qa.q: What did Rukmini first bring Baljeet?
qa.a: Murukku, her Amma's.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel at the Pongal lunch?
qa.a: She felt her shoulders loosen and felt welcome and at ease for the first time since arriving.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that returned the welcome?
qa.a: She shared her mother's pinnis door to door, starting with Rukmini, and thanked her for the murukku and Pongal.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see her gifts and invitations?
qa.a: As a real welcome, telling Baljeet she's one of them now and inviting her to the next festival.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new hostel reading shared sweets and invitations as warm welcome and returning it in her own way.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: Anjali beta, you're moving to Pune next week, so listen to your Pooja Mausi. When I was nineteen, I moved to Shillong for college, alone, into a rented room. The very first evening, the landlady's daughter came up with a plate of rice cakes and tea, and asked me a hundred questions. Where was I from, did I have brothers, did I eat pork? I thought she was nosy. I gave short answers and shut the door. The next week, the neighbours invited me to a Christmas dinner, and I almost made an excuse. Then my classmate Iba told me, "In our families, feeding you and asking about your family is how we say welcome." I felt so small. So I went, and I brought laddoos from home. They sang, they fed me, and I stayed till midnight. Take the tea, beta. The questions are the welcome.

qa.q: What did the landlady's daughter bring on the first evening?
qa.a: A plate of rice cakes and tea.

qa.q: How did young Pooja feel after Iba explained the questions?
qa.a: She felt small and ashamed of having read the kind questions as nosiness.

qa.q: What choice in the story opened the door to friendship?
qa.a: Young Pooja chose to go to the Christmas dinner and brought laddoos, instead of making an excuse.

qa.q: How did the neighbours seem to feel when young Pooja came?
qa.a: They were warm and welcoming, singing and feeding her until midnight.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city learning to read food and questions as signs of welcome shaped by local custom.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: Lavanya arrived at Pune station at eleven at night in pouring rain, and her suitcase had gone to Mumbai by mistake. She stood soaked outside her new paying-guest building, holding only a backpack. The owner's son, Chetan, came down with an umbrella. "Come in. Amma says you'll eat with us tonight." Lavanya hesitated. She didn't want to be a burden; at home you'd refuse at least twice. "No, no, I'll manage." Chetan laughed. "In this house, if you refuse, Amma will send food to your room anyway." Upstairs, his mother handed her a dry towel, a borrowed kurta and a plate of hot poha. "You're our guest first, tenant later." Lavanya felt her eyes sting. She thanked them again and again. Chetan's mother waved it away. "Just say it once. Then eat." The next morning, Chetan went with her to the courier office to chase the suitcase.

qa.q: Where had Lavanya's suitcase gone by mistake?
qa.a: To Mumbai.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when Chetan's mother gave her the towel and poha?
qa.a: She was moved and grateful, her eyes stinging, after arriving soaked and alone.

qa.q: What helped Lavanya read the invitation as real welcome?
qa.a: Chetan's joke that his mother would send food anyway, and the warm, practical care upstairs.

qa.q: How did Chetan's mother see Lavanya's repeated thanks?
qa.a: She waved it away, suggesting in her family thanks is said once, and care doesn't need repeated gratitude.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new city under difficult circumstances reading invitations and food as welcome, with custom shaping how thanks is voiced.

subtype: Grateful, welcoming and joyful in new communities [Interpreting]
passage: On Rajni's third night at the working women's hostel in Bengaluru, someone knocked with a steel plate of holige, still warm. "My amma sent a whole box," said Sharmila from the next room. "You're from Jaipur, no? Try." Rajni hesitated. In her old flat, neighbours never knocked unless something was wrong. Was this a welcome, or just extra sweets? She thanked Sharmila twice, perhaps too formally. Sharmila waved it away. "Arre, no thank-you between neighbours." The next evening Rajni found a note under her door: "Rangoli on the terrace, Sunday. Come." On Sunday she climbed up, unsure, and five women made space on the mat without a word, handing her a tin of coloured powder. Nobody thanked anyone for anything; they simply passed things along. On Monday Rajni bought a box of ghevar near the bus stand and left it on Sharmila's shelf, with no note. That night Sharmila texted one line: "Ghevar! Now you're one of us."

qa.q: What sweet did Sharmila bring?
qa.a: Holige, still warm.

qa.q: Why did Rajni hesitate at Sharmila's knock?
qa.a: Rajni felt unsure and a little wary, since in the old flat neighbours only knocked when something was wrong.

qa.q: How did Rajni learn to return the welcome?
qa.a: By joining the terrace rangoli and then leaving ghevar on Sharmila's shelf, showing thanks through sharing, the way the hostel did.

qa.q: How did Sharmila see Rajni's repeated thanks?
qa.a: As unneeded formality between neighbours, since for her gratitude is shown by sharing, not saying 🙂

grounding: It illustrates a young adult in a new city reading shared sweets and invitations as welcome, and learning how local custom shapes the way thanks is expressed.
